patients.summary: Licensed practical nurse with recurrent depression, chronic migraine, IBS-D and quiescent epilepsy who joins in 2020; later factitious diarrhea and surreptitious sulfonylurea hypoglycemia lead to a diagnosis of factitious disorder imposed on self. Toxic epidermal necrolysis from lamotrigine in 2024, three episodes of serotonin syndrome 2025 to 2026, and a pregnancy ending in severe preeclampsia with pulmonary edema and preterm cesarean in January 2026.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
29F here to establish. LPN, works days at a rehab and skilled nursing facility. Married, no kids. Prior office records reviewed (scanned 9/14).

Depression: recurrent, first episode in her early 20s. On sertraline 100 mg for years, feels it works. Mood 'okay, work is a lot right now.' No SI. Not in counseling at present. PHQ-9 7, GAD-7 5.

Migraine: chronic, no aura. Mother has the same. Uses sumatriptan 100, usually works within an hour. Estimates 6 to 8 doses a month. Discussed medication-overuse headache and prevention; she would rather keep things as they are for now.

IBS-D: years of loose stools with stress, loperamide a few times a month. No blood, no weight loss, no nocturnal stools. Sister has IBS too.

Epilepsy: seizures as a teenager, treated in childhood, off meds since about age 18 and seizure-free since. Does drive. Maternal aunt has epilepsy.

PSH: lap appy 2015.
FHx: mother depression and migraine; maternal aunt epilepsy; father HTN; sister IBS.
SH: never smoker, no alcohol, no drugs.
Allergy: sulfa (rash).

Exam: well appearing, pleasant. Vitals as charted. HEENT unremarkable. Neck supple, no thyromegaly. Heart RRR without murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, healed laparoscopic port scars. No edema. Neuro: CN intact, strength and reflexes symmetric, gait normal. Affect a little flat but appropriate.

A/P
1. MDD, recurrent - stable on sertraline 100 mg, will take over prescribing. Counseling list given.
2. Chronic migraine without aura - sumatriptan PRN; headache diary. Revisit prevention if frequency climbs.
3. IBS-D - loperamide PRN.
4. Epilepsy, in long remission off meds - no action.
5. Health maintenance: CBC, CMP, lipids, TSH; HIV and hep C screen once, she agrees. Pap due 2021. Flu shot next month at our nurse clinic (she usually gets it at work, will do it here this year).
RTC 6 months.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: loose stools x about 2 months.

HPI: Since mid-July has had watery stools most days, she counts 4 to 6 a day, worse than her usual IBS pattern which was a couple of loose days a week. Some crampy lower abdominal discomfort before BMs. No blood, no black stools, no mucus. No nighttime stools that wake her. Appetite fine, weight steady. documents.title: Colonoscopy Report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE GASTROENTEROLOGY - COLONOSCOPY REPORT (received by fax)
Date of procedure: 11/29/2022
Indication: chronic watery diarrhea
Allergies: sulfa
Sedation: monitored anesthesia care
Prep: good (BBPS 8)

The scope was passed to the cecum and the terminal ileum was intubated for about 5 cm. The ileal mucosa looked normal. Throughout the colon the mucosa was normal in appearance with a normal vascular pattern. No polyps, ulcers or masses. Random biopsies taken from the right and left colon and from the terminal ileum. Retroflexion in the rectum unremarkable.

Impression: normal colonoscopy to the terminal ileum; biopsies sent to look for microscopic colitis.
Plan: follow up pathology; stool studies to be sent; clinic visit in about 6 weeks.

documents.title: Gastroenterology Consultation
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE GASTROENTEROLOGY - CLINIC LETTER
Date of service: 01/09/2023
Re: Karen Hurley, DOB 12/22/1990
Referred by: primary care physician

Thank you for asking us to see Ms. Hurley, a 32 year old LPN, for chronic diarrhea.

She describes half a year now of watery stools, five or six a day, with occasional cramping. No blood and no mucus. She has not traveled, has had no sick contacts and has not changed her diet. Background of IBS with diarrhea, depression, chronic migraine and remote epilepsy. Medicines: sertraline 100 mg daily, sumatriptan 100 mg as needed, loperamide as needed. Allergy: sulfa (rash). Family: sister with IBS.

On exam today she looks well. Abdomen is soft without tenderness or distension.

Data: stool culture and ova and parasites negative (primary care, 9/2022). Tissue transglutaminase IgA negative. Colonoscopy to the terminal ileum 11/29/2022 normal, with random biopsies showing no microscopic colitis.

Stool studies collected 12/28/2022:
- stool osmolality 260 mOsm/kg
- serum osmolality 290 mOsm/kg
- stool sodium 30 mEq/L, stool potassium 40 mEq/L
- stool magnesium 5 mg/dL
- stool phosphate 4 mg/dL

Calculated stool osmotic gap 290 - 2 x (30 + 40) = 150 mOsm/kg.

Assessment: the measured stool osmolality is lower than plasma. Stool leaving the colon is never hypotonic to plasma, so a value like this tells us the sample has been diluted with water or another dilute fluid after passage. The gap is not interpretable for that reason, and the stool magnesium is not elevated, so I do not suspect a magnesium-containing laxative. With an otherwise complete and negative evaluation, the findings are most consistent with factitious diarrhea.

I discussed the results with her in a straightforward way. She was upset and disagreed. I have recommended a psychiatric evaluation and would ask primary care to help with that. No further GI testing planned; she can continue loperamide for her IBS symptoms. Happy to see her again if anything new develops.

Gastroenterology attending

documents.author: PCP

She asked to talk about the GI letter. Read it together. She is hurt by it, says she has been sick for months and 'nobody believes nurses.' I told her I was not there to accuse her of anything, that the test result is what it is, and that I care how she is doing either way. Stools now 'a bit better.' PHQ-9 10, no SI, no plan, safe at home with her husband.

Exam: vitals as charted, weight stable. Tearful at times, organized, linear.

A/P
1. Factitious diarrhea per GI evaluation. Offered referral to psychiatry; she declines for now. Left the door open.
2. MDD recurrent, PHQ-9 up to 10. Continue sertraline 100; she will think about counseling. Recheck 2 to 3 months.
3. IBS-D: loperamide as needed.

AREA MEDICAL CENTER, EMERGENCY SERVICES - PHYSICIAN RECORD (received by fax)
Arrival 04/05/2023 11:35, discharged from ED observation 04/06/2023 13:20

CC: spells of confusion, sweating and shakiness.

32 y/o F, LPN, known factitious diarrhea per GI evaluation this January, who reports roughly two months of intermittent spells: she gets foggy and confused, sweaty and tremulous, sometimes with a racing heart. Most happen late morning. Today a coworker found her confused at the nurses' station and checked a glucose. She takes sertraline, sumatriptan when needed and loperamide when needed and says she takes nothing else; no insulin or diabetes pills at home, no alcohol, no drugs. Allergies: sulfa.

Exam: vitals in normal range on arrival. Anxious, diaphoretic forehead, otherwise unremarkable; nonfocal neuro exam once glucose corrected.

ED course: point-of-care glucose 40 mg/dL during the spell. Critical sample drawn (insulin, C-peptide, sulfonylurea screen) before 25 g IV dextrose, with prompt return to baseline. Placed on a dextrose infusion and observed overnight with hourly checks; infusion weaned and fingersticks stayed normal for 8 hours off it. BMP unremarkable. A1c 5.2%.

Impression: hypoglycemia, cause pending. No diabetes. Send-out tests pending at discharge.
Disposition: home with husband; eat regularly; follow up with PCP within one week. The patient was told the ED would call with results.

Emergency medicine attending

documents.title: ED Addendum - Send-out Results
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
ADDENDUM 04/10/2023 (received 04/11)
Results from the critical sample drawn 04/05 during glucose 40: insulin elevated, C-peptide elevated, sulfonylurea screen positive. Together these show hypoglycemia from a sulfonylurea, which is not one of her prescribed medicines. I called the patient and reviewed the result; she denies taking one. Given the prior factitious diarrhea, I strongly recommended psychiatric evaluation and faxed this to her PCP.

2. MDD recurrent - continue sertraline 100 for now; psychiatry to advise.

Call in 2 weeks to touch base.

conditions.label: Factitious disorder imposed on self (Munchausen syndrome)

documents.title: Psychiatry Evaluation
documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
OUTSIDE PSYCHIATRY - INITIAL EVALUATION
Date of service: 04/26/2023
Referral: PCP, after hypoglycemia with positive sulfonylurea screen

Ms. Hurley is a 32 year old married LPN with a long history of recurrent depression on sertraline. Over the past nine months she has had diarrhea that GI found to be produced by dilution of stool samples, and this month an ED visit for hypoglycemia with high insulin, high C-peptide and a positive sulfonylurea screen. In session she did not offer an explanation for either finding and became tearful when they were reviewed. There is no outside gain we can identify: no leave from work, disability claim or legal matter. She denies any wish to die. She described feeling calmer when she is being looked after as a patient.

MSE: casually dressed, cooperative, guarded at first. Mood 'embarrassed.' Affect constricted, tearful. Thought process linear. No SI or HI. No psychosis. Insight partial, judgment fair.

Diagnoses: factitious disorder imposed on self, based on two objectively documented episodes of falsified illness without outside gain; major depressive disorder, recurrent.

Plan: weekly psychotherapy with our clinic; psychiatry follow-up monthly at first. Continue sertraline 100 mg daily; we will prescribe from here on. Safety plan completed. With her permission we will coordinate with her PCP; we asked that one physician hold her medical care and that new testing be ordered thoughtfully.

Outpatient psychiatrist

documents.title: Neurology Consultation
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE NEUROLOGY - HEADACHE CLINIC LETTER
Visit 07/17/2023

Dear colleague,

I saw Ms. Hurley, 32, for chronic migraine. She has had migraine since her teens and, over the past year, headaches on about 15 days a month. Sumatriptan helps the attacks it is used for; she has not had lasting control with as-needed treatment alone. She also has depression and factitious disorder followed by psychiatry, IBS with diarrhea, and epilepsy in remission off medication for more than ten years. Allergy: sulfa.

General and neurological examinations are normal today.

She met criteria for, and consented to, our crossover study of an investigational preventive. Each participant takes the study medicine for three months and a matching placebo for three months; neither she nor the treating team knows the order. Headache days are counted monthly from an electronic diary. She keeps sumatriptan for attacks.

I will write again when she completes the six months.

Headache neurologist

events.reason: Fever, sore throat and blistering skin eruption

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
TERTIARY MEDICAL CENTER - DISCHARGE SUMMARY (received 02/05/2024)
Admitted 01/14/2024 via ED to the burn and critical care unit; dermatology consulting. Discharged 02/01/2024.

Principal diagnosis: toxic epidermal necrolysis, attributed to lamotrigine.

History: 33 year old woman with factitious disorder imposed on self and prior factitious diarrhea, recurrent depression, chronic migraine, IBS-D and epilepsy, who had three days of fever and sore throat before a painful red rash appeared on her chest and back. Over about a day it spread to the face and limbs, with flaccid blisters and skin coming away. Lamotrigine 25 mg daily had been started by her outside psychiatrist about two weeks before, as an add-on for depression. Other medicines: sertraline 100 mg daily, sumatriptan 100 mg as needed, loperamide 2 mg as needed. Known allergy: sulfa (rash).

Admission exam: T 38.9 C, HR 110, BP 100/60. Dusky macules coalescing into flaccid bullae and sheets of epidermal detachment over the face, trunk and extremities, about 35% of body surface area. Nikolsky sign positive. Erosions on the buccal mucosa. Both conjunctivae injected.

Admission labs: WBC 15.0, hemoglobin 13.2, platelets 250; creatinine 1.2; ALT 45, AST 47.

Course: lamotrigine stopped on arrival and listed as an allergy. Managed in the critical care unit with warmed room, IV fluids, non-adherent dressings, eye lubrication with daily eye checks, mouth care and scheduled pain control, with nutrition support. Creatinine came back to normal with fluids. Fever settled in the first week. Re-epithelialization was steady and nearly complete by discharge. No infection. Her eyes were comfortable at discharge.

Discharge medicines: sertraline 100 mg daily; sumatriptan as needed; loperamide as needed; bland emollient to healed areas.
Allergies at discharge: LAMOTRIGINE - toxic epidermal necrolysis; sulfa - rash.
Advice: never take lamotrigine again; tell every prescriber and pharmacist. Follow up with PCP within a week and with dermatology in one month.

Hospital medicine attending, for the inpatient team

documents.title: Dermatology Inpatient Consultation
documents.author: dermatology
documents.body:
DERMATOLOGY CONSULT (inpatient, 01/14/2024; received with the discharge packet)
Reason: blistering eruption with fever.

Three days of fever and throat pain, then a painful eruption starting on the trunk, now face, trunk and limbs, with blisters and sloughing. New medicine: lamotrigine, about two weeks.

Exam: febrile and tachycardic. Confluent dusky erythema with flaccid bullae and denuded areas, positive Nikolsky sign; estimated 35% BSA detachment. Buccal erosions. Bilateral conjunctival injection.

Impression: toxic epidermal necrolysis, lamotrigine the culprit drug.
Recommendations: stop lamotrigine and record as a permanent allergy; critical care level supportive care; ophthalmic lubrication and daily eye exams; wound care as per protocol.

documents.title: Husband calling
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Pt's husband called to let us know she was admitted Sunday to the burn and critical care unit at a tertiary hospital for a severe skin reaction, thought to be from a new medicine. Message to PCP. Records request faxed for discharge summary.

documents.title: Post-hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Discharged 2/1 after 18 days for toxic epidermal necrolysis from lamotrigine. I did not know lamotrigine had been started; psychiatry added it in late December for mood.

Today: skin tender in a few spots on the back and thighs, otherwise healed over, new skin pink. Eyes a little gritty in the mornings, using drops. Mouth fine, eating normally. No fever. Tired. Husband drove her. PHQ-9 10.

Exam: vitals as charted, afebrile. Healed, re-epithelialized new skin over trunk and limbs, no open areas, no signs of infection. Conjunctivae quiet. Oral mucosa healed.

A/P
1. TEN from lamotrigine, recovering. Lamotrigine allergy on our list, flagged as high criticality. Dermatology f/u next month. Sun protection on the new skin. BMP and CBC to confirm recovery.
2. Depression - psychiatry has seen her since discharge; continuing sertraline 100 only.
3. Migraine study wrapped up while she was inpatient; neurology letter to follow.
RTC 4 months.

Ms. Hurley has completed the six months of the crossover study. Headache days by month from her diary:

AREA MEDICAL CENTER, EMERGENCY SERVICES - PHYSICIAN RECORD (received 01/13/2025)
Arrival 01/09/2025 13:05. Held in the ED observation unit; discharged 01/10/2025 15:40.

CC: confused and shaky since this morning.

34 y/o F brought by her husband with about six hours of confusion, agitation and tremor. She vomited several times this morning. Husband says she has seemed more anxious all week. Her psychiatrist changed her antidepressant about a week ago; she is now on fluoxetine. She also takes sumatriptan for occasional migraines and has been using an over-the-counter cough syrup with dextromethorphan for a few days. History of factitious disorder and a prior ED visit for confusion and tremor (hypoglycemia, 2023). Allergies: lamotrigine (TEN), sulfa. Outside med list still shows sertraline 100 mg and loperamide.

Exam: T 38.9 C, HR 120, BP 160/95. Sweating, restless. Pupils dilated, reactive to light. Hyperreflexic with inducible clonus at the ankles. Oriented to self only, not to time or place.

Labs: Na 140, K 4.2, Cl 102, HCO3 24, BUN 18, Cr 0.9, glucose 98. CBC unremarkable. UA normal.

Impression: serotonin syndrome - fluoxetine with dextromethorphan and a triptan.

Course: all serotonergic drugs and the cough syrup held. IV fluids, IV lorazepam for agitation and tremor, cyproheptadine 12 mg then 2 mg every 2 hours while symptomatic, external cooling. By the next morning she was oriented, afebrile, with clonus gone.

Disposition: home. Do not take dextromethorphan. Fluoxetine stopped; her psychiatrist was called and will advise on her antidepressant. PCP follow-up within a week.

Emergency medicine attending

2. Dextromethorphan added to her allergy list as an intolerance so it flags at pharmacies. Went over other OTC products that contain it.
3. MDD - sertraline 100 per psychiatry.

REGIONAL WOMEN'S AND BIRTH CENTER - DISCHARGE SUMMARY (received 01/14/2026)
Admitted 01/06/2026, discharged 01/12/2026.

G1, admitted at 29 weeks 3 days. Chronic hypertension on labetalol 200 mg twice daily since early pregnancy. Also recurrent depression on sertraline, epilepsy in remission without medication, factitious disorder, chronic migraine, IBS-D, serotonin syndrome twice in 2025. Allergies: lamotrigine (TEN), sulfa (rash), dextromethorphan (serotonin syndrome).

Presentation: two days of swelling in both legs and passing much less urine, then sudden breathlessness overnight with pink frothy sputum.

On arrival: BP 165/110, HR 102, RR 28, SpO2 89% on room air. Crackles halfway up both lung fields. 2+ pitting edema of both legs. Brisk deep tendon reflexes.
Labs: hemoglobin 12.5, platelets 190. Creatinine 1.2 (her baseline 0.6). Albumin 2.8. Urine protein 3+.
Chest x-ray: bilateral infiltrates consistent with pulmonary edema.

Diagnoses: severe preeclampsia without HELLP features, complicated by pulmonary edema; acute kidney injury.

Course: oxygen by mask, IV furosemide with good diuresis, IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis (continued 24 hours after delivery), IV labetalol for severe-range pressures, betamethasone for fetal lung maturity. After stabilization, primary low transverse cesarean delivery on 01/07/2026 at 29 weeks 4 days; liveborn infant admitted to the NICU. Oxygen weaned by postoperative day 2. Urine output recovered and creatinine returned to normal before discharge. Incision healing well. No seizures.

Discharge medicines: labetalol 200 mg twice daily; sertraline 100 mg daily (psychiatry). Home BP twice daily; call for BP 150/100 or higher, headache, visual change or breathlessness.
Follow-up: OB in 1 week for BP and incision; PCP in 2 to 4 weeks.

Obstetrics attending

AREA MEDICAL CENTER - ICU DISCHARGE SUMMARY (received 07/06/2026)
ED arrival 06/29/2026 10:15, admitted to the ICU, transferred to the floor 07/02, discharged 07/04/2026.

35 y/o F, two earlier episodes of serotonin syndrome (01/2025, 07/2025), recurrent depression on sertraline, chronic migraine on sumatriptan as needed, chronic hypertension on labetalol, factitious disorder, epilepsy in remission, cesarean delivery in January. Allergies listed: lamotrigine (TEN), sulfa, dextromethorphan.

Husband brought her in after two hours of confusion, agitation and shaking. He told us she had been given a prescription for dextromethorphan syrup at an urgent care a few days earlier for a lingering cough.

On arrival: HR 120, BP 160/95. Diaphoretic and tachycardic. Hyperreflexia, inducible clonus, dilated pupils.
Labs: CK 5200 U/L. Creatinine 2.1. WBC 12.0, platelets 95. PT 14 s, PTT 35 s, fibrinogen 150 mg/dL, D-dimer elevated.

Diagnoses: serotonin syndrome, third episode (sertraline, dextromethorphan, sumatriptan); acute kidney injury with marked CK elevation; low platelets and low fibrinogen with elevated D-dimer, followed closely.

Course: all serotonergic drugs held. Aggressive IV fluids, IV benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine by mouth, active cooling. No intubation. Mental status normal by day 2. CK fell daily, urine output stayed adequate, creatinine improved steadily. Platelets and fibrinogen recovered without transfusion. Moved to the floor on 07/02.

Inpatient psychiatry saw her: restart sertraline 100 mg daily at discharge, no other serotonergic medicines. Neurology by phone agreed to stop sumatriptan.

Discharge medicines: sertraline 100 mg daily; labetalol 200 mg twice daily; loperamide as needed. STOPPED: sumatriptan; dextromethorphan.
Please avoid dextromethorphan, triptans, tramadol, linezolid and other serotonergic agents.
Follow-up: PCP within 1 to 2 weeks with BMP, CBC and CK; psychiatry within 1 week.

Critical care attending
